2yr-20.stem: Users pay only for compute consumed, billed per unit of usage. Which business model is the best fit?

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because charges scale with actual consumption rather than fixed access terms.
options.B: Subscription, because users buy access for a period regardless of whether they consume much.
options.C: Bundling, because negatively correlated demands are combined and sold at a discount price.
options.D: Ultra-low cost, because the firm minimizes service and sells upgrades at premium add-ons.

2yr-20.stem: A company sells a device near cost but earns margins on proprietary replacement consumables. Which model is most accurate?

options.A: Razor–razor blades, because the initial product stimulates demand for profitable complementary replacements.
options.B: Agency, because an intermediary sells on commission while the producer sets a controlled retail price.
options.C: Wholesale, because the producer sells to retailers at a fixed discount from recommended price.
options.D: Bundling, because multiple products with negatively correlated demand are sold together at discount.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance lever most directly represents the external ‘market for corporate control’ as described?

options.A: Activist investors accumulate shares to gain control and replace management in an underperforming firm.
options.B: Inside directors provide operational information and help the board understand internal performance limits.
options.C: Stock options align incentives by letting executives buy shares at a predetermined strike price later.
options.D: Boards approve budgets and oversee stakeholder relations while CEOs manage day-to-day operations.

2yr-20.stem: A listed firm adopts a provision allowing existing shareholders to buy extra shares cheaply once an acquirer crosses a threshold. What is it?

options.A: A poison pill, because dilution makes a hostile takeover materially more expensive for the bidder.
options.B: A leveraged buyout, because debt financing enables taking the firm private through share purchase.
options.C: A subscription model, because access is sold for a time period irrespective of usage volume.
options.D: A thin-market fix, because search frictions fall when transaction costs approach near zero.

2yr-20.stem: A private-equity sponsor buys all outstanding shares using borrowed money secured by the target’s assets and delists the company. This is:

options.A: A leveraged buyout, because leverage is used to purchase shares and shift ownership from public to private.
options.B: A poison pill, because shareholders can buy discounted shares once ownership crosses a threshold.
options.C: An agency model, because a retailer sells at commission while the producer controls retail pricing.
options.D: A long-tail strategy, because niche products with low unit sales accumulate into large revenue.

2yr-20.stem: Why can industry analyst recommendations be systematically biased, even when they use public filings?

options.A: Conflicts of interest can arise because analysts’ firms may have lucrative relationships with rated companies.
options.B: Conflicts of interest vanish because EDGAR filings are standardized under GAAP and publicly searchable.
options.C: Bias is eliminated when boards appoint more inside directors who can explain the firm’s internal logic.
options.D: Bias is irrelevant because ethical conduct is fully captured by legal compliance in disclosure forms.

2yr-20.stem: A platform sells countless niche digital items; each sells rarely, but collectively they generate substantial revenue. Which concept fits best?

options.A: Long tail, because near-zero marginal cost and good search aggregate many low-volume items into large sales.
options.B: Short head, because most revenue comes from a few blockbuster hits supported by heavy marketing budgets.
options.C: Winner’s curse, because paying a premium for an acquisition destroys value after deal completion.
options.D: Adverse selection, because agents misrepresent capabilities during recruitment and screening processes.

2yr-20.stem: Which platform feature most directly helps overcome ‘thin markets’ as defined in the chapter?

options.A: Digitization plus strong search and inventory tools that match buyers and sellers across time and geography.
options.B: CEO-chair duality that accelerates board decisions by concentrating authority in one senior leader.
options.C: A poison pill that deters hostile acquirers by making takeover attempts more expensive to execute.
options.D: Bundling of negatively correlated products so each customer buys a discounted multi-product suite.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet B, the contested practice is best categorized as which governance mechanism?

options.A: Executive compensation, because boards design pay packages to align managers with shareholder interests.
options.B: Market for corporate control, because hostile bids discipline managers through takeover threats.
options.C: Financial statement auditing, because GAAP compliance is verified by certified public accountants.
options.D: Long-tail innovation, because niche offerings collectively generate substantial revenue streams.

2yr-20.stem: Which pair matches the two CEO-pay issues singled out in the governance section?

options.A: Absolute CEO pay relative to average employee pay, and the pay–performance relationship’s strength.
options.B: CEO tenure relative to board tenure, and the percentage of inside directors on compensation committees.
options.C: CEO pay secrecy relative to competitors, and the frequency of SEC filings for compensation disclosure.
options.D: CEO pay volatility relative to stock volatility, and the use of bundling to sell compensation packages.

2yr-20.stem: Behavioral evidence cautions that very high-powered incentives can sometimes reduce performance mainly because they:

options.A: Distract attention toward the outsized near-term bonus and increase stress, reinforcing short-termism.
options.B: Eliminate information asymmetry by making effort perfectly observable through measurable outcomes.
options.C: Remove adverse selection by ensuring only the most capable candidates accept performance pay.
options.D: Prevent moral hazard by forcing agents to internalize all downside losses of risky projects.

2yr-20.stem: A board grants stock options with a strike price set at the grant date. Under agency theory, the primary intent is to:

options.A: Align managers with owners by tying upside to share-price appreciation above a predetermined threshold.
options.B: Guarantee dividends by reallocating profits from reinvestment into fixed quarterly shareholder payouts.
options.C: Replace the need for outside directors because managers now have identical preferences to investors.
options.D: Eliminate takeover threats because higher pay makes hostile bidders less interested in acquisitions.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why CEO-chair duality can weaken governance, even when decision speed improves?

options.A: Agenda control and friendly appointments can reduce the board’s independence in evaluating CEO performance.
options.B: Inside directors become illegal under SEC rules, so the board loses information needed for oversight.
options.C: Hostile takeovers become impossible, so the market for corporate control no longer functions at all.
options.D: GAAP standards no longer apply, so auditors cannot compare performance across firms consistently.

2yr-20.stem: A hedge fund accumulates shares and demands a spin-out to boost near-term valuation. Which shareholder-horizon fact is most relevant?

options.A: Shareholders differ: some seek long-term viability while activist funds may target short-term price movement.
options.B: Shareholders are homogeneous because each share confers identical goals and identical time preferences.
options.C: Shareholders’ goals are irrelevant because boards must legally optimize only employee welfare in all cases.
options.D: Shareholders do not vote for directors because directors are appointed by auditors under SEC authority.

2yr-20.stem: A public company’s stock price collapses; a bidder believes it can fix internal problems and launches a hostile bid. This illustrates:

options.A: The market for corporate control disciplining management when internal governance mechanisms have failed.
options.B: Adverse selection in hiring because candidates misrepresent capabilities during the recruitment process.
options.C: Long-tail dynamics because niche products accumulate into large revenues when marginal costs are low.
options.D: Bundling economics because negatively correlated products are sold together at discounted prices.

2yr-20.stem: In takeover contexts, ‘winner’s curse’ most accurately refers to situations where the acquirer:

options.A: Pays a premium that results in overpayment and subsequent shareholder value destruction.
options.B: Uses leverage to buy shares and take the company private, avoiding public disclosure obligations.
options.C: Adopts a poison pill that dilutes ownership once an acquirer crosses a threshold percentage.
options.D: Bundles two products with negatively correlated demand and sells them together at discount.

2yr-20.stem: Why have poison pills become rarer according to the chapter’s discussion?

options.A: Actively involved institutional investors often oppose pills because they hinder efficient equity-market discipline.
options.B: SEC rules have fully banned poison pills for all listed companies since the global financial crisis.
options.C: Poison pills eliminate hostile bids perfectly, so acquirers stopped attempting takeovers altogether.
options.D: Poison pills are now replaced by freemium pricing because digital services need user acquisition.

2yr-20.stem: Which act is illegal in the insider-information discussion, even though possessing insider information is part of an executive’s job?

options.A: Trading on material nonpublic information or tipping others who trade before public release.
options.B: Learning time-sensitive performance data before analysts see it in quarterly public filings.
options.C: Holding private internal data about production and demand trends as part of normal management work.
options.D: Briefing the board about nonpublic operational setbacks during a confidential governance meeting.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO uses corporate funds for extravagant personal perks that shareholders ultimately pay for. This is best described as:

options.A: On-the-job consumption, a form of agency cost enabled by information asymmetry and weak monitoring.
options.B: Adverse selection, because the CEO misrepresented capabilities during recruitment for the role.
options.C: Thin markets, because only a few suppliers can provide luxury services to executives in time.
options.D: Long tail, because many small purchases aggregate into a large overall revenue distribution.

2yr-20.stem: A firm discovers a senior hire cannot do key tasks, but effort is high. Which agency problem is most plausible?

options.A: Adverse selection, because the agent’s ability was misrepresented or misjudged before hiring.
options.B: Moral hazard, because the agent can do the work but chooses to shirk effort after hiring.
options.C: Winner’s curse, because the firm overpaid for an acquisition due to bidding competition.
options.D: Poison pill, because a defense provision triggered once an acquirer crossed ownership threshold.

2yr-20.stem: A scientist can complete assigned work but instead reallocates effort to a private project. Which is the best diagnosis?

options.A: Moral hazard, because the principal cannot easily verify best effort despite the agent’s capability.
options.B: Adverse selection, because the scientist’s skills were exaggerated during recruiting and screening.
options.C: Short head, because the firm depends on a few blockbuster innovations rather than many small ones.
options.D: Wholesale, because the firm sells through retailers at a fixed discount to recommended prices.

2yr-20.stem: A manager says: “Our new charging-fee policy is legal, so ethics is irrelevant.” Which correction is closest to the text?

options.A: Legal actions can still be ethically questionable; ethics involves societal norms like fairness and reciprocity.
options.B: If legal, the action is necessarily fair; markets enforce fairness automatically through customer choice.
options.C: Ethics is only for nonprofits; for-profit firms optimize shareholder returns regardless of moral norms.
options.D: Ethics equals compliance; therefore ethics analysis can be outsourced entirely to the legal department.

2yr-20.stem: Which action best illustrates ‘ethical pursuit of competitive advantage’ as a foundation for long-run performance?

options.A: Designing growth targets that can be met legally while rewarding transparent reporting and safe problem solving.
options.B: Driving short-term stock spikes through aggressive goal pressure even when legal ambiguity is exploited.
options.C: Hiding risks in complex disclosures as long as GAAP is followed and penalties remain unlikely.
options.D: Replacing codes of conduct with performance bonuses to signal that results matter more than process.

2yr-20.stem: A carmaker sells the vehicle and then sells recurring software upgrades and service subscriptions. Which model best captures the upgrade logic?

options.A: Razor–razor blades, because the initial sale can stimulate ongoing purchases of complementary high-margin add-ons.
options.B: Wholesale, because dealers buy at discount and set retail prices independently to earn resale margins.
options.C: Agency, because independent agents sell and take commissions while the producer controls the retail price.
options.D: Bundling, because negatively correlated product demands are combined and sold at a discount.

2yr-20.stem: A company charges a monthly fee for access regardless of how much the service is used. Which business model is this?

options.A: Subscription, because users pay for access during a term whether or not usage is high.
options.B: Pay-as-you-go, because billing scales strictly with measured consumption volume in each period.
options.C: Freemium, because the basic tier is free while premium tiers monetize advanced capabilities.
options.D: Ultra-low cost, because a stripped service is cheap and upgrades are sold at premium prices.

2yr-20.stem: A firm bills only per kWh consumed at charging stations. Which model fits best?

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because the user pays only for the measured consumption of the service.
options.B: Subscription, because the user buys access for a time period regardless of actual consumption.
options.C: Wholesale, because retailers earn a margin over fixed discounts from recommended retail prices.
options.D: Agency, because commissions are paid to intermediaries who sell at controlled retail prices.

2yr-20.stem: Which bundling condition is most essential in the chapter’s example of the Office suite?

options.A: Demand is negatively correlated so different users value different components more, enabling discount bundles.
options.B: Demand is perfectly correlated so every user values every component equally, maximizing willingness to pay.
options.C: Supply is scarce so bundling reduces inventory costs through physical shelf space optimization only.
options.D: Demand is random so bundling makes price discrimination impossible and therefore increases piracy.

2yr-20.stem: A platform sells millions of niche accessories that individually sell rarely, but collectively matter. This is best described as:

options.A: Long tail, where many low-volume items add up when shelf space and distribution costs approach zero.
options.B: Short head, where most revenue comes from a few blockbuster hits supported by large marketing budgets.
options.C: Winner’s curse, where takeover premiums cause acquirers to destroy value after integration challenges.
options.D: Moral hazard, where agents shirk effort because principals cannot observe effort after contracting.

2yr-20.stem: Which external mechanism most directly strengthens governance by standardizing disclosure and enabling outsider scrutiny?

options.A: SEC filing requirements plus audits under GAAP, which enable analysts to examine standardized statements.
options.B: CEO-chair duality, which accelerates decision-making by unifying oversight and operational authority.
options.C: Bundling, which increases customer willingness to pay by packaging negatively correlated products.
options.D: Freemium, which lowers adoption barriers by giving away basic features to attract users.

2yr-20.stem: An investment bank’s analysts rate their own client firms more favorably. The best interpretation is:

options.A: A conflict of interest that can bias external monitoring even when the information is publicly available.
options.B: A proof that GAAP is ineffective because accounting standards allow any narrative to pass audits.
options.C: A reason to increase inside directors because external monitors cannot ever be objective.
options.D: A demonstration that ethics is culture-specific and therefore cannot be evaluated across firms.

2yr-20.stem: A company shifts from selling boxed software to cloud access that reduces piracy by monitoring logins. Which model shift is most accurate?

options.A: A move toward subscription and cloud delivery that alters revenue timing and reduces piracy through monitoring.
options.B: A move toward wholesale distribution that lets retailers set price and profit from resale margins.
options.C: A move toward a poison-pill defense that deters hostile acquirers by diluting their ownership stake.
options.D: A move toward long-tail selling that earns most revenue from niche items rather than popular hits.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance mechanism is most ‘internal’ according to the chapter’s phrasing about ethics and control?

options.A: Business ethics embedded in culture and leadership cues that guide behavior beyond formal monitoring.
options.B: A poison pill that dilutes hostile bidders once they cross an ownership percentage threshold.
options.C: An LBO that shifts ownership from public shareholders to private equity sponsors via leverage.
options.D: Analyst coverage that reacts to quarterly filings and publishes buy/hold/sell recommendations.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best matches the board–CEO relationship described in the governance section for public companies?

options.A: The CEO reports to the board; the board approves budgets and oversees stakeholder issues and CEO performance.
options.B: The board reports to the CEO; the CEO approves budgets and appoints directors to monitor stakeholder issues.
options.C: The board replaces the CEO in daily operations; directors run units directly to reduce information asymmetry.
options.D: The CEO reports only to auditors; boards exist mainly to file SEC statements and manage disclosure timing.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet C, which external governance mechanism is most directly at work?

options.A: Government regulators enforcing compliance obligations and penalties for violations of financial laws.
options.B: Inside directors increasing information flow to the board, reducing managerial opportunism directly.
options.C: Stock options aligning manager incentives with shareholders through predetermined strike prices.
options.D: Bundling products with negatively correlated demand to increase willingness to pay across segments.

2yr-20.stem: A compliance function is under-resourced because growth bonuses dominate. Which concept best diagnoses the systemic problem?

options.A: Bad barrel: the organizational climate and incentives normalize corner cutting beyond individual bad actors.
options.B: Bad apple: a few employees broke rules, so replacing them is sufficient regardless of incentive design.
options.C: Thin markets: compliance staff and leadership cannot find each other to coordinate in time and space.
options.D: Long tail: many small compliance failures add up to a large revenue stream from niche customers.

2yr-20.stem: An exchange operator knows far more than customers about custody risk but markets itself as ‘risk-free.’ This most directly reflects:

options.A: Information asymmetry that can enable opportunism unless governance and ethics constrain claims.
options.B: Poison-pill protection that deters hostile takeovers through share dilution at ownership thresholds.
options.C: Leveraged-buyout incentives that shift ownership to private equity through debt-financed share purchases.
options.D: Bundling benefits that arise when products have negatively correlated demand across customer segments.

2yr-20.stem: A compliance officer can do the work but chooses to underinvest effort because penalties will fall on the firm, not the individual. This is:

options.A: Moral hazard, because hidden effort and shifted costs increase incentives to shirk responsibility.
options.B: Adverse selection, because the officer misrepresented capability during hiring and screening.
options.C: Winner’s curse, because overpayment for an acquisition destroys value after integration.
options.D: Short head, because revenue depends primarily on a few blockbuster products, not niche variety.

2yr-20.stem: A manager says: “We complied with the letter of the law, so ethics is satisfied.” Which response best matches the chapter?

options.A: Law is a minimum standard; ethical evaluation can still judge actions questionable under societal norms.
options.B: Ethics equals legal compliance; therefore ethical analysis is redundant once counsel signs off.
options.C: Ethics is culture-relative only; therefore universal norms like honesty cannot guide business conduct.
options.D: Ethics is an external audit function; therefore internal codes of conduct are unnecessary.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance response most directly reduces information asymmetry between insiders and outsiders in a regulated financial platform?

options.A: Standardized public reporting plus independent auditing and regulator oversight of disclosures and controls.
options.B: Increasing CEO-chair duality to unify command and speed decisions in volatile markets.
options.C: Adding more inside directors only, to ensure the board receives richer internal operational updates.
options.D: Switching from pay-as-you-go fees to subscription pricing to stabilize revenue predictability.

2yr-20.stem: A platform charges fees per transaction; heavy users pay more, light users pay little. Which model is the best fit?

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because pricing scales with actual consumption of the service (transactions).
options.B: Subscription, because payment is tied to access over time regardless of usage intensity.
options.C: Wholesale, because intermediaries set final prices and profit from resale margins.
options.D: Bundling, because negatively correlated preferences allow discounting across multiple products.

2yr-20.stem: A platform offers basic trading tools free, but charges for advanced analytics and priority support. Which model is closest?

options.A: Freemium, because a free base expands adoption while premium add-ons monetize power users.
options.B: Ultra-low cost, because minimal service is cheap and upgrades are sold at premium a la carte.
options.C: Agency, because an intermediary sells at commission while the producer controls retail pricing.
options.D: Wholesale, because retailers set price and profit from a fixed discount to recommended price.

2yr-20.stem: A crypto wallet app is free, but the firm earns margins on proprietary swaps and withdrawals. Which model is most precise?

options.A: Razor–razor blades, because the free core stimulates recurring purchases of profitable complements.
options.B: Bundling, because multiple products with negatively correlated demand are sold together at discount.
options.C: Wholesale, because retailers buy at a discount and set their own final prices for consumers.
options.D: Poison pill, because discounted share purchases deter takeover attempts by diluting bidders.

2yr-20.stem: Offering thousands of low-volume tokens while relying on search and recommendation to match niche demand is closest to:

options.A: Long tail, where many niche offerings aggregate into substantial revenue when marginal costs are low.
options.B: Short head, where a few blockbuster tokens drive almost all revenues through mass marketing budgets.
options.C: Moral hazard, where agents shirk effort because principals cannot observe post-contract behavior.
options.D: Adverse selection, where candidates misrepresent ability during recruitment and screening.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best explains how digital platforms can overcome thin markets in niche assets?

options.A: They reduce transaction costs and search frictions so dispersed buyers and sellers can find each other.
options.B: They centralize decision rights in a CEO-chair to speed governance and reduce dissent in oversight.
options.C: They deter hostile takeovers through poison pills that dilute acquirers beyond ownership thresholds.
options.D: They bundle negatively correlated products so each user buys more even if they want only one.

2yr-20.stem: A public crypto firm’s shares fall sharply; activists accumulate stock and push for leadership change. Which mechanism is operating?

options.A: Market for corporate control, where control contests discipline underperforming management.
options.B: Executive compensation, where stock options align incentives by tying pay to future share prices.
options.C: Board composition, where inside directors provide operational detail to help monitor management.
options.D: Business ethics, where values statements guide behavior beyond legal compliance requirements.

2yr-20.stem: A firm adopts a poison pill. Which trade-off noted in the chapter helps explain why such defenses are controversial?

options.A: They deter hostile bids but can hinder equity-market discipline, so institutional investors often oppose them.
options.B: They deter bids and also reduce SEC disclosure, so analysts cannot evaluate firms accurately anymore.
options.C: They deter bids and also eliminate winner’s curse, so acquisitions become value-creating by default.
options.D: They deter bids and also create long tails, so niche products become the main revenue source.

2yr-20.stem: A private sponsor uses leverage to buy a listed exchange and take it private, aiming to restructure and later re-list. This is:

options.A: A leveraged buyout, which changes ownership from public to private using borrowed money.
options.B: An agency model, where a retailer sells on commission while the producer controls retail pricing.
options.C: A freemium model, where the basic service is free but premium features are paid add-ons.
options.D: A bundling model, where negatively correlated products are discounted when sold together.

2yr-20.stem: Which action is most clearly illegal under the insider-trading discussion in the governance section?

options.A: Trading securities based on material nonpublic information or tipping another trader before disclosure.
options.B: Learning internal transaction volume trends before they appear in the firm’s quarterly public reporting.
options.C: Discussing nonpublic risk controls with the board during confidential governance oversight meetings.
options.D: Collecting operational data faster than competitors through legitimate analytics and data infrastructure.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO’s lavish personal spending using company funds is best framed as which agency cost?

options.A: On-the-job consumption enabled by information asymmetry and weak monitoring controls.
options.B: Adverse selection because capability was unknown before appointment and screening was imperfect.
options.C: Winner’s curse because a takeover premium caused overpayment and post-deal value destruction.
options.D: Thin markets because few luxury suppliers exist, raising transaction costs and scarcity pricing.

2yr-20.stem: A firm issues a code of conduct but rewards rule-bending quietly. The chapter suggests employees will most likely:

options.A: Follow observed executive actions because informal culture and incentives outweigh slogans and duplicity is visible.
options.B: Follow the written code because formal statements override daily rewards and punishments automatically.
options.C: Ignore both because ethics is solely personal and cannot be shaped by organizational context.
options.D: Act ethically if and only if auditors explicitly test ethics adherence in annual financial statements.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best represents business ethics as defined in the chapter?

options.A: An agreed-upon code of conduct in business grounded in societal norms, beyond legal minimums.
options.B: A personal belief system that cannot be shared across cultures and therefore cannot guide firms.
options.C: A set of SEC regulations specifying how firms must format disclosures under GAAP principles.
options.D: A pricing policy that maximizes profit given customer willingness to pay in competitive markets.

2yr-20.stem: A firm’s leadership sets revenue targets that can only be met by evading controls. The chapter suggests the most likely outcome is:

options.A: Increased corner cutting and potential illegal behavior because top-down pressure and high stakes distort choices.
options.B: Higher ethical performance because intense goals always induce discipline and eliminate moral hazard.
options.C: Lower information asymmetry because ambitious goals increase transparency through frequent reporting.
options.D: Lower short-termism because hard goals force leaders to focus on long horizons rather than quick wins.

2yr-20.stem: A business model is described as ‘strategy in action.’ Which statement is closest to the chapter’s meaning?

options.A: It translates how to compete into a blueprint of tactics, target market, and monetization logic.
options.B: It replaces strategy because tactics and goals are identical once the firm selects a target segment.
options.C: It is the same as corporate governance because boards and auditors implement strategy directly.
options.D: It is a takeover defense because it prevents hostile bidders from acquiring the firm cheaply.

2yr-20.stem: Which prompt in the business model framework most directly asks about value creation in economic terms?

options.A: Why does the model create value through its revenue streams and cost structure choices?
options.B: What activities must be performed to create and deliver the offering reliably to customers?
options.C: Who are the stakeholders performing activities from suppliers through partners to customers?
options.D: How are activities linked and sequenced to create and deliver the offering at scale and quality?

2yr-20.stem: A platform sells a few megahits and also many niche items using recommendation systems. The chapter implies it can:

options.A: Earn from short head plus long tail, because technology expands selection while still selling blockbusters.
options.B: Earn only from the long tail, because blockbusters disappear when recommendation engines are used.
options.C: Earn only from the short head, because niche items cannot aggregate unless physical inventory exists.
options.D: Avoid thin markets only with poison pills, because takeover defenses create buyer-seller matching.

2yr-20.stem: Which principle is most consistent with the MBA oath excerpt discussed in the ethics section?

options.A: Managers should not advance personal interests at the expense of the enterprise or society.
options.B: Managers should maximize personal compensation as a proxy for shareholder value creation.
options.C: Managers should treat law and ethics as identical because only codified rules matter.
options.D: Managers should avoid reporting risks to prevent panic and maintain market confidence.

2yr-20.stem: Which neglected business-model framework question most directly explains a compliance breakdown when KYC is outsourced to partners?

options.A: Who, because unclear stakeholder responsibility for core activities creates gaps in execution and accountability.
options.B: Why, because revenue and cost logic alone determines whether compliance controls are implemented effectively.
options.C: What, because listing activities is sufficient even if no party is accountable for performing them.
options.D: How, because process linkage is irrelevant if partner roles and accountability are not specified.

2yr-20.stem: Agency theory views the firm as a ‘nexus of legal contracts.’ Which implication is most consistent with that view?

options.A: Conflicts are addressed through incentives and monitoring embedded in contracts, with disputes often resolved legally.
options.B: Conflicts are eliminated by culture alone, because shared values substitute fully for formal monitoring mechanisms.
options.C: Conflicts are irrelevant in for-profit firms, because shareholder value automatically aligns every stakeholder’s goals.
options.D: Conflicts vanish once disclosures are public, because information asymmetry disappears under standardized reporting.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet D, which business-model weakness most directly undermines the ‘Why’ question in the framework?

options.A: Revenue timing and cost commitments are mismatched, so unit economics fail when occupancy drops.
options.B: Stakeholder roles are unclear, so the firm cannot identify who performs key activities reliably.
options.C: Activities are unlinked, so services cannot be delivered at all even when demand is strong.
options.D: Legal compliance is unclear, so ethics becomes impossible to evaluate across cultural contexts.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best fits the principal–agent concern often present in high-growth real estate startups like in Caselet D?

options.A: Managers may pursue growth, prestige, and personal benefits even when it increases risk borne by owners.
options.B: Owners may pursue personal perks even when it increases risk borne by managers and employees.
options.C: Customers may pursue insider trading profits even when it increases risk borne by suppliers and partners.
options.D: Auditors may pursue long-tail revenue even when it increases risk borne by activist investors.

2yr-20.stem: If a listed coworking firm’s stock collapses and activists seek control to ‘fix’ mismanagement, the chapter would label this as:

options.A: Market for corporate control, an external governance mechanism that disciplines underperformance.
options.B: Executive compensation, an internal mechanism that aligns incentives through stock option grants.
options.C: Inside directorship, an internal mechanism that improves information flow from management to board.
options.D: Bundling, a business model that sells negatively correlated products together at a discount.

2yr-20.stem: A bidder pays a large premium for a distressed coworking chain and later destroys value. The chapter’s term for this is:

options.A: Winner’s curse, because takeover premiums can cause overpayment and subsequent value destruction.
options.B: Poison pill, because shareholders dilute the bidder once it crosses an ownership threshold.
options.C: Freemium, because basic access is free while premium add-ons monetize advanced features.
options.D: Thin markets, because few buyers and sellers exist and cannot find each other in time and space.

2yr-20.stem: A founder markets an IPO narrative that is technically legal but arguably misleading about unit economics. Which statement aligns with the chapter?

options.A: Actions can be legal yet ethically questionable, because ethics extends beyond minimum legal standards.
options.B: If legal, the narrative is necessarily ethical, because disclosure law defines societal norms completely.
options.C: Ethics cannot be applied to business models, because business models are purely technical blueprints.
options.D: Ethics is solved by stock options, because equity incentives guarantee honesty in communication.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet D, which ‘bad barrels’ mechanism is most plausible when employees feel pressured to misstate occupancy metrics?

options.A: Leadership cues and unrealistic targets normalize misreporting, so context drives unethical behavior widely.
options.B: A few employees are bad apples; replacing them fixes ethics without changing targets or incentives.
options.C: Thin markets prevent accurate occupancy tracking because buyers and sellers cannot find each other.
options.D: Long tail explains misreporting because many small errors aggregate into a large revenue distribution.

2yr-20.stem: The chapter suggests CEOs are held to high ethical standards partly because:

options.A: CEO reputation is a critical asset, and unethical behavior can quickly destroy legitimacy and trust.
options.B: CEO reputation is irrelevant once auditors verify GAAP compliance in financial statements.
options.C: CEO reputation can be replaced by aggressive growth targets, which signal competence to markets.
options.D: CEO reputation is controlled only by activists, so boards have little role in ethical expectations.

2yr-20.stem: A coworking firm charges members a fixed monthly fee for access to spaces, regardless of how many hours they use. This is:

options.A: Subscription, because payment is for access during a term rather than strictly for measured usage.
options.B: Pay-as-you-go, because charges scale precisely with hours used and metered consumption.
options.C: Freemium, because the base access is free while premium features are paid add-ons.
options.D: Wholesale, because the firm sells access to retailers at discounts who set their own prices.

2yr-20.stem: If the firm instead bills per desk-hour used, the closest business model label is:

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because charges track actual consumption rather than time-based access rights.
options.B: Subscription, because users pay for a period regardless of how much they consume.
options.C: Bundling, because services with negatively correlated demand are packaged at discount prices.
options.D: Agency, because third-party agents sell the desk-hours at commission while firm sets prices.

2yr-20.stem: A coworking chain offers ultra-cheap basic space but charges high prices for meeting rooms and amenities. This is closest to:

options.A: Ultra-low cost, because stripped basic service is cheap and extras are sold at premium a la carte.
options.B: Freemium, because basic service is free while premium tiers monetize advanced capabilities.
options.C: Wholesale, because retailers buy at a discount and set final prices to earn resale margins.
options.D: Poison pill, because takeover deterrence is created through share dilution triggers.

2yr-20.stem: A firm bundles workspace, mail handling, and coffee into one package at a discount because different customers value different components. This is:

options.A: Bundling, because negatively correlated demand across components allows discounting that expands willingness to pay.
options.B: Razor–razor blades, because the initial product is sold cheaply to drive recurring replacement purchases.
options.C: Agency, because an intermediary sells on commission while the producer controls the retail price.
options.D: Long tail, because many niche products aggregate into large revenue when shelf space is unlimited.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance mechanism is most relevant when management wants to avoid takeover threats after poor performance?

options.A: Poison pill adoption, though it can impede equity-market discipline and thus face investor opposition.
options.B: Freemium adoption, because free tiers deter acquirers by raising customer switching costs.
options.C: Long-tail adoption, because niche assortment makes acquisition integration too complex to attempt.
options.D: GAAP elimination, because weaker standards reduce transparency and thus deter bidders.

2yr-20.stem: A private-equity firm buys a listed coworking company using debt secured by assets, takes it private, then plans an IPO later. This is:

options.A: A leveraged buyout, because leverage is used to purchase shares and change ownership from public to private.
options.B: A poison pill, because dilution triggers deter hostile bidders once ownership crosses a threshold.
options.C: A wholesale model, because retailers set prices and earn margins over discounted publisher prices.
options.D: A freemium model, because base service is free while premium add-ons monetize advanced features.

2yr-20.stem: Which pair of statements best captures how auditors and the SEC contribute to governance in public firms?

options.A: They enforce standardized disclosures and audits, enabling outsider scrutiny for irregularities and strategy signals.
options.B: They set product prices and bundles, enabling firms to match negatively correlated preferences at discount rates.
options.C: They appoint directors and chairs directly, ensuring boards are independent from managers by regulation alone.
options.D: They eliminate information asymmetry entirely, making agency problems disappear in publicly traded companies.

2yr-20.stem: A bank’s analysts rate their own clients too favorably. Which governance risk is highlighted by the chapter?

options.A: Conflicts of interest can bias external monitors even when information is public and standardized.
options.B: Conflicts of interest are impossible because all firms file EDGAR reports and thus are perfectly comparable.
options.C: Bias is solved by increasing inside directors, because internal knowledge makes external judgment unnecessary.
options.D: Bias proves ethics is irrelevant, because markets only reward performance and ignore monitoring quality.

2yr-20.stem: Which scenario is the cleanest illustration of adverse selection within an employment relationship?

options.A: A candidate exaggerates their ability to manage leases and later cannot execute core tasks.
options.B: A hired manager reallocates effort to a personal venture because monitoring is weak after hiring.
options.C: A bidder overpays for an acquisition due to a premium and later destroys shareholder value.
options.D: A platform struggles to match rare buyers and sellers because search costs are high offline.

2yr-20.stem: Which scenario best illustrates moral hazard rather than adverse selection?

options.A: A capable manager chooses to underinvest effort in tenant retention because performance is hard to observe.
options.B: A job candidate misstates experience in commercial real estate during recruitment and is hired.
options.C: A bidder pays an acquisition premium and later realizes synergies were overestimated during bidding.
options.D: A retailer sells only short-head hits because carrying long-tail inventory is too costly physically.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO uses company funds for personal luxury items while asking employees to cut costs. This is best labeled:

options.A: On-the-job consumption, a manifestation of agency costs under information asymmetry.
options.B: Thin markets, because luxury suppliers are rare and cannot be found easily in time and space.
options.C: Bundling, because multiple consumption items are packaged together under one corporate account.
options.D: Long tail, because many small purchases aggregate into large overall revenue for suppliers.

2yr-20.stem: A board removes a CEO after ethical controversy even without proof of illegal behavior. The chapter’s logic suggests this is because:

options.A: Ethical leadership sets the tone; CEOs under scrutiny must meet high standards to sustain trust and culture.
options.B: Only illegal behavior matters; therefore board actions without illegality are irrational and unethical.
options.C: Ethics is purely cultural; therefore boards cannot judge CEO conduct using any shared standards.
options.D: Ethics is solved by market for corporate control; boards should wait for activists to intervene.

2yr-20.stem: After Chapter 11, a firm is taken private and stops filing quarterly SEC reports. Which external governance lever weakens most directly?

options.A: Industry analysts’ scrutiny based on standardized public filings, because less disclosure reduces outsider monitoring.
options.B: Inside directors’ access to operational details, because private status prohibits managers from joining boards.
options.C: CEO-chair duality, because private ownership legally requires separating the chair and CEO roles.
options.D: Bundling’s pricing advantage, because private firms cannot sell bundles without public reporting duties.

2yr-20.stem: A turnaround board appoints an independent chair and adds outside directors with no prior ties to the CEO. Which agency concern is targeted most directly?

options.A: Reducing CEO influence over agendas and evaluation, strengthening monitoring where information asymmetry is high.
options.B: Eliminating adverse selection in hiring by screening candidates after employment begins through close oversight.
options.C: Preventing winner’s curse by lowering takeover premiums paid in acquisitions of distressed competitors.
options.D: Solving thin markets by increasing the number of buyers and sellers through recommendation algorithms.

2yr-20.stem: A restructuring plan links executive bonuses to occupancy but reduces payouts if safety, churn, or complaint indicators worsen. Which principle is being applied?

options.A: Incentive alignment that discourages short-termism by balancing growth metrics with risk and quality constraints.
options.B: A pure pay-as-you-go model that charges executives only for the hours they work on strategic initiatives.
options.C: A poison pill that deters hostile bidders by diluting their ownership once a threshold is crossed.
options.D: A long-tail strategy that shifts bonuses toward niche segments because blockbusters distort incentives.

2yr-20.stem: A new policy requires pre-approval for entertainment expenses and audits travel and vendor bills. Which agency cost is this policy most directly designed to curb?

options.A: On-the-job consumption and perquisites, which shareholders ultimately finance when monitoring is weak.
options.B: Adverse selection, which occurs when candidates misrepresent capability during recruitment and screening.
options.C: Winner’s curse, which occurs when acquirers overpay due to takeover premiums and later destroy value.
options.D: Thin markets, which occur when too few buyers and sellers exist to match supply and demand efficiently.

2yr-20.stem: Why is a ‘long tail’ business model structurally harder to replicate in physical coworking than in digital media platforms?

options.A: Physical capacity and location costs remain high, so marginal distribution is not near zero and selection is constrained.
options.B: Recommendation engines cannot be used in services, so demand cannot be matched across segments at all.
options.C: Bundling cannot work in services, so negatively correlated preferences cannot be aggregated into a single offer.
options.D: Agency theory does not apply to services, so principals cannot contract with agents to deliver offerings.

2yr-20.stem: Which diagnosis best separates a compelling narrative strategy from a fragile business model in Caselet D’s setting?

options.A: A strong story can attract demand, but if revenue logic cannot cover fixed commitments, the business model fails.
options.B: A strong story guarantees profits, because customer enthusiasm always offsets fixed cost commitments.
options.C: A business model is only a mission statement, so narrative and economics are effectively the same thing.
options.D: A business model is a takeover defense, so narrative matters only if it deters hostile acquirers.

2yr-20.stem: In a public stock company, which ‘first-principles’ contract best explains why a board exists at all?

options.A: A state charter grants limited liability; shareholders elect a board that then hires and monitors executives, in practice.
options.B: A CEO contract mandates quarterly growth; analysts enforce it, and employees elect a board to meet targets, overall.
options.C: A supplier contract grants financing; suppliers elect the board to secure repayment and set executive pay, in practice.
options.D: A consumer contract guarantees refunds; customers elect the board to oversee product and marketing claims, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page frames the corporation around a state charter and limited liability, after which shareholders elect a board to hire and monitor top management. The other options misplace who elects the board and confuse governance with contracts for performance, suppliers, or refunds.

2yr-20.stem: A founder hides that a flagship demo is nonfunctional until after investors commit funds. Which agency problem label fits best?

options.A: Adverse selection, because hidden information before contracting causes principals to buy a ‘lemon’ asset, in practice, in practice.
options.B: Moral hazard, because hidden action after contracting shifts risk to principals while agents enjoy upside, as stated here.
options.C: Perquisite consumption, because managers misuse resources on private benefits rather than firm objectives, for this case, in practice.
options.D: Thin markets, because too few buyers and sellers exist to match supply and demand at scale, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Adverse selection is the hidden-information problem that occurs before the transaction. The Nikola example on the course page illustrates investors buying a ‘lemon’ due to concealed facts. Moral hazard is post-contract hidden action, not pre-contract concealment.

2yr-20.stem: A bank officer issues unauthorized guarantees for kickbacks after the loan relationship is in place. Which agency label fits best?

options.A: Moral hazard, because hidden action after contracting increases risk borne by the principal while the agent benefits, overall.
options.B: Adverse selection, because hidden information before contracting causes the principal to select a low-quality agent, as stated here.
options.C: Winner’s curse, because overpaying in a takeover leads to value destruction after the acquisition closes, as stated here.
options.D: Bundling, because combining products increases willingness to pay when preferences are negatively correlated, for this case, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page treats the PNB/Nirav Modi episode as moral hazard: hidden action after contracting, where the agent takes risks or commits misconduct while the principal bears losses. Adverse selection is pre-contract. The other options belong to M&A or business models.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO cuts next‑gen R&D in Q4 to hit earnings and trigger a personal bonus, harming long‑term viability. This is best read as:

options.A: An agency cost driven by misaligned incentives, where short‑term payoffs induce decisions that reduce long‑term value, as stated here.
options.B: An adverse selection problem, where investors cannot observe capability and therefore hire an unqualified CEO initially, as stated here.
options.C: A thin market problem, where too few buyers exist for R&D outputs to justify continued investment and talent hiring.
options.D: A long‑tail strategy, where small sales across many niche products replace blockbuster returns in innovation spending, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: This matches the classic agency-cost logic highlighted in the course simulation: incentive contracts tied to short-term results can induce managerial short‑termism. It is not adverse selection (pre‑hire screening), nor a demand-side niche strategy for product variety.

2yr-20.stem: Agency theory describes the firm primarily as which type of entity?

options.A: A nexus of legal contracts that must manage conflicts of interest through monitoring and incentive alignment, in practice.
options.B: A social community in which values alone eliminate opportunism, making formal monitoring mechanisms unnecessary, in practice, in practice.
options.C: A production function in which scale efficiencies guarantee alignment because profits automatically discipline agents, in practice, in practice.
options.D: A political arena in which regulators set strategy, leaving boards to execute rules rather than oversee managers, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook explicitly frames agency theory as viewing the firm as a nexus of legal contracts, with governance mechanisms needed to align principals and agents. Culture matters, but agency theory does not claim culture alone eliminates opportunism.

2yr-20.stem: In the Waymo–Uber episode, which governance failure is most directly illustrated?

options.A: Moral hazard by a rogue agent exploiting access to proprietary assets once trusted, absent sufficient monitoring and controls.
options.B: Adverse selection by principals choosing a bad technology platform because network effects hid quality differences pre‑deal, in practice.
options.C: Market for corporate control failure because hostile takeover defenses blocked a merger that would have prevented theft, overall.
options.D: Bad‑barrel culture because every employee was forced to cheat, making individual choice largely irrelevant throughout, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page frames the case as moral hazard: hidden action after trust is granted, where an agent exploits assets for personal gain. It is not adverse selection, takeover defenses, or a ‘everyone cheats’ systemic-pressure story.

2yr-20.stem: Which board composition is most likely to strengthen monitoring in a high‑uncertainty startup with charismatic leadership?

options.A: A majority of independent outside directors with relevant domain expertise and the authority to challenge management claims, as stated here.
options.B: A majority of inside directors drawn from top management to maximize information flow and ensure unified decision making, in practice.
options.C: A board dominated by celebrity outsiders who expand access to capital even if they lack time to study operating details.
options.D: A board composed mainly of major suppliers, because suppliers face the highest risk and therefore monitor best, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats the board as the central internal governance mechanism for public firms and emphasizes monitoring and oversight. Independent outside directors can challenge management and reduce capture, particularly when information asymmetry and charisma are high.

2yr-20.stem: When a CEO also serves as chair of the board, the most precise governance concern is:

options.A: Reduced board independence because agenda-setting and evaluation power concentrates, weakening oversight of the top agent, as stated here.
options.B: Reduced managerial initiative because separation of roles is required for speedy decision making and market responsiveness, in practice.
options.C: Reduced audit quality because CEO-chair duality legally blocks independent auditors from issuing unqualified opinions, in practice, in practice.
options.D: Reduced market competition because duality automatically triggers antitrust concerns in concentrated industries, as stated here, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: CEO-chair duality can weaken oversight by consolidating leadership and monitoring roles in one individual. The other options incorrectly link duality to legal audit prohibitions or market structure effects.

2yr-20.stem: Which example best reflects ‘on‑the‑job consumption’ as an agency cost rather than adverse selection or moral hazard?

options.A: Senior managers charge lavish personal travel and entertainment to the firm, reducing shareholder value without improving strategy, overall.
options.B: A founder misrepresents product functionality before fundraising, causing investors to buy a low-quality asset, in practice, in practice.
options.C: Traders increase leverage after receiving guarantees that losses will be socialized, while bonus upside stays private, in practice.
options.D: A platform fails because few users exist on each side, preventing efficient matching between buyers and sellers, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: On-the-job consumption refers to perquisites and private benefits extracted by agents. The other options are adverse selection, moral hazard, or thin-market dynamics.

2yr-20.stem: A board wants to reduce information asymmetry without becoming an operating committee. Which action best fits that goal?

options.A: Require standardized reporting dashboards and independent internal audits while keeping day‑to‑day decisions with management, in practice, as stated here.
options.B: Replace senior managers with directors as interim operators until all operational processes are fully stabilized and standardized, in practice.
options.C: Eliminate all variable pay so managers have no incentive to manipulate targets, relying solely on fixed salaries for alignment.
options.D: Outsource governance to rating agencies and analysts, because external scrutiny can fully substitute for internal oversight, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The governance challenge is to monitor without micromanaging: standardized reporting and independent assurance can reduce asymmetry while preserving managerial responsibility. The other options either overreach into operations or assume incentives/externals alone solve agency issues.

2yr-20.stem: In a hierarchy, the principal–agent problem ‘cascades’ most accurately because:

options.A: Each manager is both an agent to superiors and a principal to subordinates, creating layered incentive and monitoring challenges.
options.B: Only CEOs are agents, while all other employees are principals because they control day‑to‑day decisions and information flows, overall.
options.C: Shareholders directly manage employees through stock markets, so the cascade is mainly an illusion in modern corporations, in practice.
options.D: Regulators act as principals to boards, so the cascade runs from government to directors to shareholders to employees, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook notes that principal–agent issues extend beyond shareholders and CEOs: managers at each level delegate and monitor, creating cascading agency problems through the hierarchy.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why governance mechanisms must include both monitoring and incentives?

options.A: Monitoring reduces hidden action and misreporting, while incentives align payoffs so agents prefer principal-valuing choices over time, in practice.
options.B: Monitoring eliminates all information asymmetry, while incentives are irrelevant once agents face constant scrutiny in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Monitoring is only for fraud detection, while incentives only matter for innovation and never for ethics or compliance choices.
options.D: Monitoring is external by definition, while incentives are internal by definition, so they cannot be designed coherently together, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: Governance is about directing and controlling: monitoring limits opportunism and information distortion, while incentives shape choices where monitoring is imperfect. The other options either overclaim perfect monitoring or artificially separate governance tools.

2yr-20.stem: A founder recruits a board mostly for prestige and fundraising access, not for oversight capacity. Which agency risk rises most?

options.A: Managerial entrenchment and weak monitoring, because symbolic directors may lack time, expertise, or independence to challenge claims, overall.
options.B: Underinvestment in marketing, because prestige directors typically demand higher advertising spend that crowds out brand building, in practice.
options.C: Improved disclosure quality, because prestige directors increase transparency incentives to protect their reputations automatically, in practice, in practice.
options.D: Lower transaction costs in takeovers, because prestige boards attract acquirers and remove the need for premiums entirely, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: A prestige-heavy board can become ineffective at oversight, increasing agency costs under information asymmetry—an issue highlighted by the Theranos-style pattern of high-profile boards without relevant monitoring depth.

2yr-20.stem: A startup claims ‘everyone exaggerates early metrics’ to justify selective reporting that misleads investors. Which distinction is most central?

options.A: Legal compliance is a minimum standard; conduct can be legal yet unethical, and deception can cross into fraud when material facts are hidden.
options.B: Ethics and law are identical standards, so if the startup avoids prosecution the practice is necessarily ethically acceptable, in the scenario, in practice.
options.C: Ethics is only personal morality, so corporate disclosures are outside ethics and belong only to finance and regulation fields, as framed, in practice.
options.D: Fraud requires direct physical harm, so misleading financial or product claims cannot be fraud without patient injuries, as described, in this context, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: Both the textbook and course page emphasize that ethics is broader than law, and that misrepresentation of material information can become criminal fraud even when actors rationalize it as ‘startup storytelling.’

2yr-20.stem: Which governance response is most directly aimed at reducing adverse selection in hiring rather than moral hazard in performance?

options.A: Strengthening screening and verification before contracting, such as reference checks, skill tests, and independent credential validation, on balance, in practice.
options.B: Linking compensation to long-term outcomes, such as deferred equity vesting, so managers internalize future downside risks, on balance, in practice.
options.C: Installing continuous monitoring systems, such as audits and dashboards, to detect hidden actions and misreporting after hiring, as stated here.
options.D: Designing a poison pill, such as share dilution triggers, to deter hostile bidders from acquiring the firm at a premium.

2yr-20.explanation: Adverse selection is pre-contract hidden information; screening before hiring targets it. The other actions address moral hazard or takeovers, not pre-hire selection.

2yr-20.stem: A firm’s board approves the annual budget and evaluates the CEO’s performance. This is best understood as:

options.A: A central internal governance mechanism that directs and controls the enterprise while leaving daily operations to management, overall.
options.B: A substitute for external regulation, because once budgets are approved regulators no longer oversee listed firms in practice.
options.C: A market-for-control function, because budget approval is the same as initiating hostile takeovers to discipline managers, in practice.
options.D: A business model choice, because budgeting is primarily about pricing tactics and customer segmentation rather than oversight, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook describes the board as a key internal governance mechanism: it oversees the company broadly, approves major plans such as budgets, and monitors the CEO, while managers run operations.

2yr-20.stem: An executive argues: ‘Because our incentive plan uses stock options, agency problems disappear.’ Which correction is most accurate?

options.A: Stock-based pay can align interests, but it can also intensify short-termism or risk-taking if metrics and vesting horizons are poorly designed.
options.B: Stock-based pay guarantees honesty, because market prices instantly reflect true performance and punish misreporting quickly, overall, as described, as stated here.
options.C: Stock-based pay is irrelevant, because agency problems exist only between employees and customers rather than owners and managers, as stated here.
options.D: Stock-based pay causes adverse selection, because investors cannot observe effort and therefore must overpay for equity compensation, as described, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page flags CEO compensation divergence and the textbook treats incentives as helpful but imperfect: design matters, and stock-based pay can still create distortions, especially with short horizons.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best distinguishes governance from strategy in this chapter’s framing?

options.A: Governance sets mechanisms to direct and control, while strategy specifies goal-directed actions; business models translate strategy into action.
options.B: Governance is the same as strategy, because boards choose products and pricing and managers simply execute without judgment.
options.C: Strategy is only ethics and compliance, while governance is only marketing and product design, so they operate independently.
options.D: Governance concerns customers and suppliers, while strategy concerns shareholders and boards, so they rarely overlap in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter positions governance as mechanisms to direct and control; strategy as goal-directed competitive actions; and business models as the translation of strategy into action. The other options invert or separate these concepts incorrectly.

2yr-20.stem: When a board is ‘captured’ by a powerful founder, which remedy most directly increases independent oversight without removing expertise?

options.A: Add independent outside directors with relevant expertise and empower them through committee leadership and agenda rights, in practice.
options.B: Replace all outside directors with insiders to increase coordination and reduce dissent that slows rapid market entry, overall.
options.C: Stop using audits to avoid creating fear, because psychological safety is enough to prevent manipulation and misreporting, overall.
options.D: Shift to a pure freemium model so customer growth substitutes for governance credibility in capital markets and regulation.

2yr-20.explanation: Capture reduces oversight; adding independent expertise and real authority strengthens monitoring while preserving domain knowledge. The other options either worsen capture, remove assurance, or confuse governance with business models.

2yr-20.stem: Which pairing is correctly matched to the timing of the underlying agency problem?

options.A: Adverse selection: before the transaction; moral hazard: after the transaction, when behavior is hard to observe, in practice.
options.B: Adverse selection: after the transaction; moral hazard: before the transaction, when screening is incomplete, in practice, in practice.
options.C: Adverse selection: only in takeovers; moral hazard: only in retail pricing and bundling decisions for customers, in practice.
options.D: Adverse selection: only in ethics scandals; moral hazard: only in accounting rules such as GAAP and audit standards.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page defines adverse selection as hidden information before contracting and moral hazard as hidden action after contracting. The other pairings scramble timing or misplace the concepts into unrelated domains.

2yr-20.stem: A founder insists on secrecy and restricts internal data access to a tiny group, claiming it protects IP. Which governance concern is primary?

options.A: Information asymmetry rises, weakening monitoring and increasing the chance that bad news is delayed, distorted, or suppressed, overall.
options.B: Supplier power rises, because secrecy reduces the firm’s bargaining position and automatically increases input prices, as stated here.
options.C: Threat of substitutes rises, because secrecy signals weak differentiation and invites entry with alternative technologies, as stated here.
options.D: Rivalry rises, because secrecy always triggers price wars as competitors respond to uncertainty with aggressive discounting, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Restricting information access can heighten information asymmetry between agents and principals, degrading monitoring—central to agency theory. The other answers shift into five forces rather than governance.

2yr-20.stem: Which decision most clearly belongs to directors (as directors) rather than to managers (as managers) under this chapter’s description?

options.A: Evaluating and, if necessary, replacing the CEO when performance or integrity failures threaten strategic goals and legality, overall.
options.B: Choosing daily discount levels for each city to match competitor pricing and stabilize conversion rates in short windows.
options.C: Designing product features and sprint priorities for the next release to maximize user engagement and retention in practice.
options.D: Negotiating individual supplier delivery schedules and optimizing warehouse picking routes to reduce unit costs and spoilage, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter assigns the board oversight responsibilities: monitoring the CEO and ensuring strategic goals are pursued legally. Operational and product decisions belong to management.

2yr-20.stem: A company creates a ‘values poster’ but keeps incentive metrics that reward rule-bending. Which diagnosis is most consistent with the chapter?

options.A: Governance and ethics are intertwined; without aligned incentives and controls, stated values become cosmetic rather than internalized, as described, in practice.
options.B: Values posters substitute for monitoring, because norms automatically prevent misconduct when written clearly and displayed prominently, on balance, as stated here.
options.C: Ethics depends only on individual virtue, so incentives and controls do not affect behavior and cannot be part of the diagnosis.
options.D: Compliance is identical to ethics, so as long as rules are technically followed the incentive structure is irrelevant in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter argues that ethical culture and governance controls must reinforce each other; misaligned incentives can create a ‘bad barrel’ even with lofty slogans.

2yr-20.stem: If a board wants to reduce opportunistic ‘asset grabbing’ by key employees, which control is most directly relevant?

options.A: Stronger access controls and monitoring over critical proprietary assets, paired with clear sanctions and enforcement mechanisms, in practice.
options.B: A shift to bundling unrelated services, because bundling increases customer switching costs and therefore deters employee theft, overall.
options.C: A shift to long-tail assortment, because selling niche products reduces competition and therefore eliminates opportunistic behavior, in practice.
options.D: A shift to hostile takeover defenses, because poison pills deter acquirers and therefore deter employee misappropriation of IP.

2yr-20.explanation: Asset misappropriation is a governance and control issue: access controls, monitoring, and credible enforcement reduce opportunity. The other options confuse governance controls with customer pricing or takeover defenses.

2yr-20.stem: Which reform best targets ‘agent–principal’ misalignment while preserving entrepreneurial risk-taking in a startup?

options.A: Use multi-metric incentives with longer horizons and credible monitoring, so speed and innovation are rewarded without rewarding deception, overall.
options.B: Eliminate all monitoring to preserve founder autonomy, because surveillance always reduces creativity and therefore destroys innovation, as stated here.
options.C: Replace the board with advisers only, because advisers can provide expertise while removing oversight that slows decisions in practice.
options.D: Remove outside investors entirely, because agency problems occur only with shareholders and never with employees or customers, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Balanced incentives and monitoring can preserve entrepreneurial drive while reducing incentives for deception and short-termism. Removing monitoring or oversight invites agency costs; removing investors does not remove agency problems within the hierarchy.

2yr-20.stem: Why is the market for corporate control described as a ‘last resort’ governance mechanism in the textbook?

options.A: Hostile takeovers carry high transaction costs and often require premiums that can trigger overpayment and value destruction, overall.
options.B: Hostile takeovers are legally banned for public companies, so boards must rely solely on internal monitoring mechanisms, overall.
options.C: Hostile takeovers always improve governance, so they are used only when firms are already performing exceptionally well, overall.
options.D: Hostile takeovers replace auditing and regulation, so they are the default mechanism for ensuring GAAP compliance, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook notes that corporate control markets are costly and often involve takeover premiums, creating winner’s-curse risk. They are useful when internal governance fails, but they are not costless or universally beneficial.

2yr-20.stem: In hostile takeovers, the ‘winner’s curse’ refers most precisely to:

options.A: Paying a large premium to win control and then destroying value because the acquisition price exceeds realizable gains.
options.B: Winning market share via bundling and then losing margins because customers overconsume low-priced bundle components, as stated here.
options.C: Winning a price war via ultra-low cost and then losing because rivals imitate fixed-asset ownership and scale advantages.
options.D: Winning trust via transparency and then losing because disclosure reduces competitive advantage by revealing trade secrets, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook defines winner’s curse in corporate control as overpaying—often due to takeover premiums—leading to value destruction. The other options describe unrelated business model or competition dynamics.

2yr-20.stem: A ‘poison pill’ is best defined in the chapter as:

options.A: A defensive provision designed to deter hostile takeovers by making the target firm less attractive to the acquirer, as stated here.
options.B: A whistleblower policy designed to deter internal fraud by granting anonymity and legal support to employees reporting issues, as stated here.
options.C: A pricing tactic designed to deter entry by setting an introductory price below cost and then raising it after rivals exit.
options.D: A regulatory penalty designed to deter misreporting by forcing executives to repay bonuses after accounting restatements, on balance, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter defines a poison pill as a takeover defense that makes acquisition less attractive. It is not a whistleblowing policy, a predatory pricing tactic, or a regulatory clawback rule.

2yr-20.stem: Which external governance mechanism is most directly enabled by SEC disclosure and the EDGAR database?

options.A: Industry analyst scrutiny of standardized filings, which can reveal irregularities and shape buy-hold-sell recommendations, in practice, in practice.
options.B: Supplier monitoring of inventory levels, which can enforce shorter payment cycles and raise bargaining power automatically, in practice.
options.C: Customer monitoring of product roadmaps, which can enforce faster innovation cycles and eliminate switching costs over time, overall.
options.D: Employee monitoring of executive behavior, which can enforce ethics because internal audiences always deter misconduct in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook explains that SEC filings are made available via EDGAR, enabling analyst scrutiny and external monitoring. This is not primarily a supplier/customer/employee monitoring mechanism.

2yr-20.stem: GAAP and independent audits matter as governance mechanisms primarily because they:

options.A: Reduce misrepresentation risk by standardizing reporting and requiring verification by certified public accountants, for this case, in practice.
options.B: Increase product differentiation by ensuring firms can advertise audited financials as a premium feature to customers, in practice.
options.C: Eliminate agency problems by making all managerial actions observable, so incentives and boards become unnecessary, as stated here.
options.D: Prevent hostile takeovers by reducing volatility, so acquirers cannot justify takeover premiums in capital markets, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter links GAAP and audits to the integrity of financial statements, reducing misrepresentation and supporting external monitoring. They do not eliminate agency problems nor block takeovers mechanically.

2yr-20.stem: The textbook cautions that industry analysts and credit-rating agencies may face conflicts of interest because:

options.A: They can have lucrative relationships with firms they evaluate, biasing ratings and recommendations in subtle ways, on balance, as stated here.
options.B: They are legally prohibited from reading EDGAR filings, so they rely on rumors and therefore cannot be independent, as stated here.
options.C: They are required to own shares of the firms they cover, so their personal wealth always moves with the stock price.
options.D: They are paid only by regulators, so they must please regulators rather than investors, creating systematic pessimism, as described, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter notes that analysts and rating agencies can have business relationships with the companies they evaluate, creating conflicts of interest and potential bias.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement most accurately describes the role of corporate governance ratings (e.g., external watchdog ratings) in the chapter?

options.A: They provide independent assessments that inform stakeholders such as investors, insurers, auditors, and regulators, in practice, in practice.
options.B: They replace the board of directors by taking over voting rights and appointing executives in underperforming firms, overall.
options.C: They function as takeover defenses by raising acquisition costs through mandatory disclosure of bidder intentions, as stated here.
options.D: They are business models that monetize attention through subscription fees and therefore directly create competitive advantage, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter describes an industry of governance assessment that informs stakeholders; it does not claim these ratings replace boards or serve as takeover defenses.

2yr-20.stem: A distressed firm receives a hostile bid. Which board action best matches the chapter’s governance logic?

options.A: Evaluate whether internal mechanisms failed and whether the bid creates or destroys value, considering premiums and transaction costs.
options.B: Automatically accept the bid because takeovers always improve governance and therefore must raise shareholder value over time, overall.
options.C: Automatically reject the bid because boards exist to protect management, not shareholders, from external interference in practice, overall.
options.D: Delay any decision until the next quarterly filing, because EDGAR disclosure timing determines legal authority to respond, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: Takeovers can discipline underperformance but can also destroy value through overpayment and costs. The board’s role is to evaluate and decide in shareholders’ interests, not to accept or reject automatically.

2yr-20.stem: Which pairing correctly matches an external governance actor with its core function in the chapter?

options.A: Auditors: verify financial reporting; regulators: enforce securities laws; analysts: interpret filings and business news, in practice, in practice.
options.B: Auditors: set strategy; regulators: select CEOs; analysts: approve annual budgets and hire senior managers directly, as stated here.
options.C: Auditors: design compensation; regulators: write business models; analysts: implement operational controls in departments, for this case, in practice.
