options.D: Auditors: deter entry; regulators: lower supplier power; analysts: reduce substitutes by strengthening differentiation, for this case, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter describes auditors, regulators, and analysts as external governance mechanisms supporting disclosure integrity and monitoring. The other options misassign roles or substitute industry-structure logic for governance.

2yr-20.stem: A company threatens litigation against investigative journalists and refuses to share verifiable evidence with auditors. Which external mechanism is being undermined first?

options.A: Independent information intermediation, because reporting and auditing are channels that surface hidden facts to outsiders, as stated here.
options.B: The poison pill, because litigation threats automatically trigger dilution provisions that prevent hostile bids from closing, in practice.
options.C: The long tail, because investigative scrutiny reduces niche discovery and therefore shrinks demand for low-volume items, in practice.
options.D: The freemium funnel, because journalists influence top-of-funnel signups and therefore determine conversion rates in practice, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: By blocking journalists and resisting auditors, the firm undermines external channels that reveal information to principals and the public. Poison pills, long-tail economics, and freemium conversion are unrelated.

2yr-20.stem: A firm shifts from public to private ownership and reduces standardized disclosure. Which monitoring channel weakens most directly?

options.A: Analyst scrutiny based on standardized filings, because less disclosure reduces outsiders’ ability to benchmark performance, as stated here.
options.B: Internal monitoring by inside directors, because private firms cannot legally appoint managers to boards at all, in practice.
options.C: Ethical culture, because private ownership automatically removes values and therefore forces misconduct in practice, in practice, in practice.
options.D: Business model innovation, because private firms cannot change pricing without quarterly SEC reporting requirements, in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Less disclosure weakens analyst-based external monitoring. Private status does not legally prevent inside directors, and ownership status does not determine ethics or business model innovation.

2yr-20.stem: Why can takeover premiums increase the probability of post‑deal value destruction even when governance improves?

options.A: High premiums raise the break‑even synergy threshold; if gains are smaller or slower, shareholders experience a winner’s curse.
options.B: High premiums reduce integration difficulty, because paying more guarantees cultural alignment and operational fit over time, in practice.
options.C: High premiums reduce agency costs, because acquiring firms can perfectly monitor targets once ownership changes hands, in practice.
options.D: High premiums reduce regulator scrutiny, because authorities assume expensive deals are carefully vetted in practice, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: A premium raises the price paid for control; if realizable gains do not cover it, value is destroyed despite any governance discipline. Paying more does not guarantee fit, perfect monitoring, or reduced scrutiny.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why audit standards and accounting rules are governance mechanisms rather than mere technicalities?

options.A: They structure credible disclosure so principals can monitor agents, reducing misrepresentation and enabling outside scrutiny, overall, as described, in practice.
options.B: They create switching costs by forcing customers to use one firm’s format, increasing lock‑in and pricing power in practice, overall.
options.C: They are competitive tactics to deter entry by making rivals’ reporting look worse, thereby lowering threat of entry over time.
options.D: They are ethical codes that replace the need for boards, because compliance automatically creates trust and virtue in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter ties GAAP and audits to credible disclosure and monitoring—governance essentials. They are not customer lock-in tactics, entry deterrence, or substitutes for boards and ethics.

2yr-20.stem: An investment bank rates a client’s stock unusually positively while also seeking underwriting business. Which conflict does the chapter highlight?

options.A: The evaluator’s incentives are compromised by commercial relationships, biasing recommendations and weakening external governance, in practice, as stated here.
options.B: The client’s cost structure is compromised by fixed assets, forcing a shift to ultra‑low cost and reducing analyst independence.
options.C: The client’s industry rivalry rises, forcing predatory pricing that makes all analyst ratings automatically optimistic in practice, in practice.
options.D: The evaluator’s legal charter is compromised, forcing shareholders to elect a new board for the bank’s clients immediately, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter cites evidence that investment bankers rate their own clients more favorably, illustrating conflicts of interest that weaken the monitoring role of analysts. The other options are unrelated.

2yr-20.stem: Which mechanism is most directly ‘external’ in the chapter’s governance taxonomy?

options.A: Industry analyst scrutiny and watchdog ratings that inform stakeholders using public information and independent assessment, overall, as described, in practice.
options.B: The board of directors choosing a CEO and approving the annual budget while monitoring management within the firm, in practice.
options.C: Corporate culture shaping norms and values so employees feel safe to speak up and leaders ‘walk the talk’ in practice.
options.D: Incentive pay contracts that link bonuses to metrics to align interests between principals and agents over time, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: Analysts and governance ratings operate outside the firm, using disclosure and assessment to monitor. Boards, culture, and incentives are internal mechanisms.

2yr-20.stem: A board adopts a poison pill during a takeover attempt (Item 16). Which risk is most plausible from an agency perspective?

options.A: Managerial entrenchment, because defenses can protect underperforming managers and reduce the disciplining effect of corporate control markets, in practice.
options.B: Reduced disclosure integrity, because poison pills replace the need for GAAP audits and therefore weaken financial statement reliability, overall.
options.C: Reduced ethical culture, because takeover defenses automatically cause pressure systems that force employees to create fake accounts in practice.
options.D: Reduced long‑tail potential, because hostile bidders cannot acquire niche assets and therefore must focus on blockbuster products only, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: A takeover defense can be value-preserving, but it can also entrench management by blocking an external discipline mechanism. The other claims misstate relationships to audits, ethics culture, or product assortment strategies.

2yr-20.stem: The chapter defines business ethics most accurately as:

options.A: An agreed-upon code of conduct in business based on societal norms that guide behavior beyond mere legal compliance.
options.B: A set of government regulations enforced by courts that fully specify acceptable behavior in every market and transaction.
options.C: A personal belief system that varies entirely by manager and therefore cannot be taught or institutionalized in organizations.
options.D: A public-relations strategy used to protect brand equity during crises, independent of governance mechanisms and incentives, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook defines business ethics as agreed-upon conduct based on societal norms. Law is a minimum, but ethics extends beyond compliance; ethics is also not reducible to PR or purely personal belief.

2yr-20.stem: Which claim best captures the chapter’s warning about ‘legal but unethical’ behavior?

options.A: Staying within the law is a minimum standard; managers can act legally while exploiting information asymmetries in ways society finds unethical.
options.B: If conduct is legal, it is automatically ethical, because laws fully encode fairness and honesty across all cultures and contexts, overall.
options.C: If conduct is ethical, it must also be legal, because ethical principles are always codified into enforceable statutes in practice, overall.
options.D: If conduct is illegal, it is always unethical, but if it is legal it is ethically neutral and therefore beyond evaluation.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook explicitly distinguishes law and ethics: legal conduct can still be ethically questionable, especially when incentives and information asymmetries enable exploitation.

2yr-20.stem: A salesforce opens unauthorized accounts to hit aggressive daily quotas. Under the chapter’s ‘bad barrels’ logic, the best diagnosis is:

options.A: Systemic pressure and incentive design created conditions where misconduct became predictable, even if individuals remain accountable, on balance, in practice.
options.B: A few immoral individuals caused the problem, so firing them solves the issue without changing systems or targets over time.
options.C: Regulators caused the problem, so reducing compliance requirements would eliminate the incentive to fabricate accounts in practice, as stated here.
options.D: Customers caused the problem, so increasing switching costs through bundling would prevent internal misconduct altogether, overall, as described, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The ‘bad barrel’ perspective emphasizes systemic drivers—targets, pressure, leadership tone—that can push many people into unethical acts. Firing individuals may be necessary but is insufficient without system redesign.

2yr-20.stem: In VW Dieselgate, the most conceptually precise reason the ‘bad barrel’ framing fits is that:

options.A: Engineers faced an impossible constraint set under performance pressure, making a workaround socially reinforced rather than purely individual deviance, in practice.
options.B: A single engineer acted alone without leadership knowledge, so system design and incentives were largely irrelevant in practice, as stated here.
options.C: The act was legal but unpopular, so it is an ethics issue only because the public disliked the technology over time.
options.D: The firm lacked a business model, so cheating substituted for strategy because pricing and positioning were unclear in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page describes the ‘iron triangle’ pressure and systemic conditions that can normalize cheating. That fits the bad-barrel logic more than a lone-actor story.

2yr-20.stem: An auditor notices a large discrepancy in bank statements (Satyam-style). Which response best reflects ethical reasoning beyond mere role compliance?

options.A: Escalate through governance channels and, if internal response fails, consider external whistleblowing to protect stakeholders from harm, in practice.
options.B: Ignore it because it is the partner’s job; role boundaries remove personal responsibility as long as tasks were completed.
options.C: Wait until quarterly results are released; public disclosure alone will force correction without internal escalation steps, as stated here.
options.D: Leak the issue anonymously to competitors; competitive pressure is a legitimate substitute for ethical reporting in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Ethical conduct requires proactive escalation when material harm is at stake; role boundaries do not eliminate moral responsibility. Waiting for markets or leaking to rivals is not a principled governance path.

2yr-20.stem: Which intervention is most consistent with building a ‘good barrel’ rather than merely punishing ‘bad apples’?

options.A: Redesign goals, incentives, and reporting so employees can meet expectations without deception, supported by leaders modeling conduct, as described, as stated here.
options.B: Issue a one-time memo on values while keeping the same sales quotas and punishment culture for those who miss targets in practice.
options.C: Increase secrecy and NDA enforcement so fewer people see problems, thereby reducing the likelihood of public scandals over time, as stated here.
options.D: Centralize decision rights in one charismatic leader to ‘set the tone,’ reducing debate and making compliance faster in practice, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: A ‘good barrel’ is created through system design, incentives, and leadership behavior that make ethical actions feasible and safe. Memos without redesign, secrecy, and centralization tend to worsen systemic risk.

2yr-20.stem: The MBA oath described in the textbook is best characterized as:

options.A: A voluntary pledge intended to professionalize management ethics, but with uncertain behavioral impact and no formal sanctions, in practice.
options.B: A legally binding document required for all managers, enforced by regulators through disbarment-like professional penalties, overall, as stated here.
options.C: A firm-level code written by boards that automatically replaces the need for compliance programs and internal controls in practice.
options.D: A marketing initiative designed to increase customer demand, with no connection to governance mechanisms or leadership conduct, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook notes the MBA oath is voluntary, seeks high ethical standards, but its effect is unknown and it imposes no consequences for misconduct.

2yr-20.stem: A manager argues: ‘We complied with emissions testing, so our actions are ethical.’ Which rebuttal best matches the chapter?

options.A: Ethics is not synonymous with compliance; designing around tests to mislead violates societal norms even if legal loopholes exist.
options.B: Ethics equals compliance, so passing tests proves ethical conduct regardless of intent or real-world consequences in practice, in practice.
options.C: Ethics is only about profitability, so if cheating protects jobs and market share it is ethically justified over time.
options.D: Ethics is only personal, so corporate intent is irrelevant and only individual beliefs should be evaluated in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter warns that legality is a minimum; exploiting loopholes or deception can remain unethical. Intent and real-world impacts matter in evaluating conduct.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO approves large loans to a group while a close family member benefits financially from that group. This is best classified as:

options.A: A conflict of interest that undermines governance credibility and ethical integrity, even if formal procedures appear to be followed.
options.B: A long-tail strategy that increases variety and therefore reduces dependence on any single borrower or industry sector over time.
options.C: A poison pill that deters hostile takeovers, because related-party transactions make the firm less attractive to acquirers in practice.
options.D: A freemium strategy that increases adoption, because loans act as free trials that later convert into profitable relationships, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The ICICI-style pattern is a classic conflict of interest: private benefit linked to corporate decisions, which undermines fiduciary norms and governance. It is not a business model or takeover defense.

2yr-20.stem: Johnson & Johnson’s Tylenol recall is used as an example of ‘good barrel’ behavior mainly because:

options.A: Leaders prioritized public safety and acted consistently with stated values despite high short-term cost, reinforcing trust norms, as described, in practice.
options.B: Leaders reduced disclosure and delayed action to avoid panic, demonstrating that secrecy is ethically superior during crises in practice, in practice.
options.C: Leaders used a poison pill to prevent activists from demanding a recall, showing that takeover defenses create ethical autonomy in practice.
options.D: Leaders shifted to a long-tail business model to replace lost sales, demonstrating that assortment is the primary ethical mechanism, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The point is values in action: prioritizing safety and trust over short-term profit aligns with ethical norms and strengthens stakeholder commitment. The other options contradict that logic or confuse ethics with takeover defenses or assortment.

2yr-20.stem: Boeing 737 MAX ‘concealment of MCAS’ (as presented in the course page) illustrates which ethical risk mechanism?

options.A: Cost and timeline pressure can incentivize concealment that shifts risk to users, making ethics a systemic design issue not a slogan.
options.B: Network effects force concealment, because platforms must hide features to avoid negative externalities and reduce multi-homing in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Ultra-low cost strategy forces concealment, because only fixed-asset ownership can reduce training costs and therefore requires secrecy, as described, in practice.
options.D: Freemium strategy forces concealment, because free users must be kept ignorant so premium conversion can occur without resistance in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page treats Boeing as a culture/pressure case: avoiding training costs and meeting timelines can push concealment that endangers stakeholders—an ethics and governance failure.

2yr-20.stem: A firm modifies products specifically for crash tests while selling different configurations to customers. This is best understood as:

options.A: Deceptive compliance that may be legalistic but violates honesty norms, fitting ‘legal vs ethical’ and ‘bad barrel’ concerns, in the scenario, overall.
options.B: A bundling tactic that increases perceived value by combining safety and performance into one offer, raising willingness to pay in practice, overall.
options.C: A subscription tactic that stabilizes demand forecasting and therefore reduces incentive to manipulate testing and reporting over time, in the scenario, overall.
options.D: A wholesale tactic in which retailers buy at a discount and therefore must manage test results to protect resale margins in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Rigging tests is deceptive compliance: it exploits the gap between formal testing and real-world performance, violating honesty and fairness norms. The other options describe pricing/contracting models unrelated to deception.

2yr-20.stem: In the FAME‑II ‘subsidy arbitrage’ example on the course page, the most precise ethical issue is:

options.A: Misrepresentation of local value addition to capture public subsidies, exploiting information gaps between firms and the state, overall.
options.B: Adverse selection by customers, because buyers choose low-quality scooters due to hidden defects in battery technology over time.
options.C: Moral hazard by consumers, because riders drive recklessly once insured, increasing accident risk borne by insurers in practice.
options.D: A long-tail strategy, because firms import many niche parts and therefore sell small volumes across diverse product variants.

2yr-20.explanation: The case is framed as misrepresentation to capture subsidies—an ethics and compliance issue involving deception toward public principals. The other options mislabel the mechanism as customer selection, insurance risk shifting, or assortment economics.

2yr-20.stem: A firm rewards ‘hockey stick’ growth and punishes dissent; employees then normalize small reporting manipulations (Item 14). Which lens fits best?

options.A: Bad barrel dynamics, because systemic pressure and leadership tone create predictable misconduct even among otherwise decent employees, overall.
options.B: Bad apple dynamics, because systemic pressure is irrelevant and only a few individuals’ greed determines misconduct in practice.
options.C: Winner’s curse dynamics, because paying a premium for growth leads to overpayment and therefore causes manipulation over time.
options.D: Long-tail dynamics, because selling less of more requires experimentation and therefore explains misreporting as innovation in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: Systemic pressure, incentive design, and tone at the top are classic ‘bad barrel’ ingredients. Misconduct can become normalized when the system punishes honesty and rewards distortion.

2yr-20.stem: In the chapter, a business model is defined most precisely as:

options.A: A blueprint that translates strategy into action by specifying tactics, target market, customer needs, and how the firm makes money.
options.B: A mission statement that describes values and purpose, while leaving tactics, target market, and revenue logic to emerge later, overall.
options.C: A governance charter that specifies director duties and audit requirements, while leaving customer value and pricing to markets, in practice.
options.D: A five-forces map that identifies entry, rivalry, substitutes, and bargaining power, while leaving revenue capture unspecified in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook defines business models as translating strategy into action: tactics and initiatives, target market and customer needs, and the revenue logic for making money. Mission, governance charters, and five forces are related but not the business model definition.

2yr-20.stem: In the business model framework (why–what–who–how), which pairing is most accurate?

options.A: Why: value proposition and rationale; Who: target customers and stakeholders; What: offerings; How: revenue and delivery logic, in practice.
options.B: Why: product features; Who: regulators only; What: board committees; How: hostile takeover defenses such as poison pills in practice.
options.C: Why: cost structure; Who: suppliers only; What: audit standards; How: analysts’ buy-hold-sell recommendations over time, overall, as stated here.
options.D: Why: legal compliance; Who: courts; What: penalties; How: prosecutions that substitute for business model design in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The framework guides leaders to define rationale/value, offerings, customers, and execution/revenue logic. The other options misplace governance and compliance items into the business model framework.

2yr-20.stem: Nespresso is presented as an example of which business model logic on the course page?

options.A: Razor-and-blade (bait-and-hook), where a durable platform is sold near cost while high-margin consumables generate profits, overall, as stated here.
options.B: Freemium, where a free version attracts users and a premium tier monetizes power users through feature gating over time.
options.C: Wholesale, where retailers buy at a discount and set resale prices, earning margin mainly through inventory turnover in practice.
options.D: Pay-as-you-go, where usage is metered and customers pay only for consumption without lock-in or proprietary complements, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page explicitly frames Nespresso as bait-and-hook: machines (bait) and proprietary pods (hook), reinforced by lock-in. That differs from freemium, wholesale, or usage-metered pay-as-you-go models.

2yr-20.stem: Country Delight is used on the course page to illustrate which primary business model advantage of subscription?

options.A: Better demand forecasting that reduces spoilage and middlemen costs, improving unit economics in a perishable supply chain, overall.
options.B: Lower threat of entry, because subscriptions legally prevent competitors from offering similar products in the same market, overall.
options.C: Lower buyer power, because subscription customers cannot cancel without regulatory approval and therefore become captive in practice, overall.
options.D: Higher supplier power, because subscriptions force farms to accept lower prices and therefore raise margins automatically over time.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page highlights subscription enabling forecasting and reduced spoilage, especially in perishables. Subscriptions do not legally block entry, nor do they make cancellation impossible; supplier power effects are not automatic.

2yr-20.stem: D‑Mart’s EDLC–EDLP model is described on the course page as relying most directly on:

options.A: Asset ownership and working-capital discipline that enable low costs and low prices, reinforced by limited SKUs and cash discounts, overall.
options.B: Freemium sampling and viral loops that enable low customer acquisition costs, reinforced by network effects and referral incentives, in practice.
options.C: Poison pills and takeover defenses that enable low costs by stabilizing control, reinforced by premium pricing and exclusivity in practice.
options.D: Long-tail assortment and infinite shelf space that enable low prices, reinforced by niche variety and algorithmic discovery over time, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page notes ownership choices, limited SKUs, and fast supplier payments to secure discounts—classic EDLC/EDLP mechanics. The other options are software platform or takeover tools or long-tail logic, not D‑Mart’s described model.

2yr-20.stem: Bundling is described on the course page as especially powerful when:

options.A: Products are negatively correlated in demand, so the bundle’s perceived value can exceed the sum of parts for many customers.
options.B: Products are perfect substitutes, so bundling reduces competition by eliminating choice and forcing single-product adoption in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Products are commodities, so bundling creates lock-in solely by raising the list price without changing willingness to pay over time.
options.D: Products are perishable, so bundling ensures forecasting accuracy and therefore eliminates spoilage without subscription commitments, overall, as described, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page emphasizes bundling negatively correlated products to create a ‘walled garden’ where value exceeds parts. Substitutes, list-price inflation, or perishability are not the core mechanism described.

2yr-20.stem: The long tail concept is best summarized (as in the course page and textbook) as:

options.A: Selling small volumes of many niche items becomes feasible when technology lowers distribution and search costs, expanding selection, as stated here.
options.B: Selling large volumes of a few blockbuster items is feasible when technology lowers distribution costs, shrinking selection in practice, in practice.
options.C: Selling niche items requires physical shelf space expansion, so long-tail success depends mainly on owning more retail real estate over time.
options.D: Selling niche items depends mainly on takeover defenses, because acquisition threats force firms to focus on blockbusters in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Long tail is ‘selling less of more’: digitization and search lower distribution frictions and enable niche demand to be served. It is not primarily about blockbusters, physical shelf space, or takeover defenses.

2yr-20.stem: Threadless (textbook) best illustrates which business model innovation mechanism?

options.A: Crowdsourcing and wisdom of crowds across the value chain, reducing downside by producing only designs validated by the community, overall.
options.B: Poison-pill governance that prevents hostile takeovers, reducing downside by avoiding acquisition premiums and winner’s curse in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Freemium pricing that converts users into paying customers by locking premium designs behind a paywall and limiting access over time.
options.D: Wholesale distribution that shifts inventory risk to retailers, reducing downside by requiring retailers to prepay for all designs in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook describes Threadless as crowdsourcing design, forecasting, and demand validation (‘I’d buy it’), producing only community-approved designs to reduce downside. The other options confuse business model innovation mechanisms.

2yr-20.stem: Which diagnosis best distinguishes ‘strategy’ from ‘business model’ in the chapter’s framing?

options.A: Strategy sets the goal-directed competitive approach; the business model specifies the tactics and revenue logic that operationalize it, in practice.
options.B: Strategy is pricing tactics; the business model is industry structure; governance then sets customer value and product positioning in practice.
options.C: Strategy is the board’s job; the business model is the regulator’s job; managers only execute without discretion in practice, overall.
options.D: Strategy is ethics; the business model is legality; governance is marketing; so each operates in separate silos over time, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter explicitly positions business models as ‘strategy in action’: translating strategic intent into concrete initiatives and revenue logic. The other options scramble the relationships.

2yr-20.stem: Dollar Shave Club is used in the chapter as evidence that disruptive advantage can come mainly from:

options.A: Business model innovation that changes economics and distribution, even when underlying product technology is not radically new, in practice.
options.B: Radical product technology that makes competitors obsolete, even when distribution and pricing remain unchanged in practice, as stated here.
options.C: Takeover defenses that prevent incumbents from acquiring entrants, making disruption legally protected over time, in practice, as stated here.
options.D: GAAP reporting differences that hide true costs, making disruption an accounting artifact rather than real value creation in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter highlights Dollar Shave Club as business model innovation disrupting an incumbent—changing how value is delivered and captured rather than relying on breakthrough blade technology.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why business models are ‘dynamic’ in the chapter?

options.A: Managers must adapt tactics, partners, and revenue logic as environments shift; a once-effective model can become obsolete over time, as stated here.
options.B: Business models never change once chosen, because stability guarantees competitive advantage and adaptation signals strategic weakness in practice, in the scenario, overall.
options.C: Business models change only when regulators rewrite accounting rules, because revenue logic is determined by GAAP rather than by design choices, overall.
options.D: Business models change only through hostile takeovers, because acquisitions are the only mechanism that can alter how firms make money in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats business models as evolving: changes in technology, competition, or customer behavior can require adaptation. They are not fixed, not determined solely by accounting, and not changed only via takeovers.

2yr-20.stem: A platform aggregator earns from ads and discovery, while a logistics-focused competitor earns from delivery fees and membership. This contrast best illustrates:

options.A: Different profit drivers within similar markets, where the ‘how’ of the business model differs even when the ‘what’ looks similar, in practice.
options.B: Different governance mechanisms, where one firm uses a poison pill and the other uses GAAP audits to create competitive advantage in practice.
options.C: Different industry structures, where one operates in monopoly and the other in perfect competition, so business models do not matter over time.
options.D: Different ethics codes, where one has values and the other lacks them, so economics follow automatically from moral superiority in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page contrasts aggregator vs logistics models (e.g., Zomato vs Swiggy) in profit drivers—how value is captured. That is a business model difference, not a governance or ethics label by itself.

2yr-20.stem: Which situation best illustrates ‘thin markets’ as a barrier to long-tail success?

options.A: Too few buyers and sellers exist in each niche, so matching is hard unless technology aggregates demand and supply across boundaries.
options.B: Too many buyers exist in each niche, so matching is easy and technology therefore cannot add value in practice, in practice.
options.C: Too many suppliers exist, so supplier power collapses and firms must rely on takeover defenses rather than matching over time, overall.
options.D: Too few regulators exist, so markets cannot function and business models must be replaced by legal enforcement in practice, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: Thin markets arise when there are too few participants for efficient matching. Aggregation and search technology can help—central to long-tail viability.

2yr-20.stem: A firm combines subscription with an ecosystem bundle. Which risk is most consistent with the chapter’s emphasis on ‘strategy in action’?

options.A: Complexity without value creation, if added tactics increase costs and confusion without improving customer value or unit economics, in practice.
options.B: Guaranteed lock-in, because adding tactics always increases switching costs regardless of customer perception in practice, overall, as described, in practice.
options.C: Guaranteed ethics, because bundling and subscription reduce incentives to misreport and therefore eliminate bad-barrel risks over time, as stated here.
options.D: Guaranteed takeover immunity, because bundled customers prevent hostile bidders from paying premiums and therefore stop corporate control markets in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats business models as translating strategy into actionable economics; adding tactics can backfire if it adds complexity without improving value or margins. Lock-in, ethics, and takeover immunity are not automatic.

2yr-20.stem: A firm offers a free tier with ads and a paid tier with premium features (Item 15). Which label fits best?

options.A: Freemium, because a free version acquires users while a paid version monetizes a subset through feature gating and convenience, overall.
options.B: Subscription only, because all recurring payments are subscriptions regardless of free tiers, ads, and conversion funnels in practice, in practice.
options.C: Wholesale only, because free tiers are equivalent to bulk discounts given to retailers who then set resale prices in practice.
options.D: Razor-and-blade only, because all recurring revenue must come from consumables rather than from upgrades and service bundles in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: A free tier plus paid upgrade is the canonical freemium structure. Subscription can be part of the paid tier, but the defining feature is the free-to-paid conversion funnel; wholesale and razor-and-blade are different logics.
